data.hypothesis: The catalog reports 10 distinct measured programs. Compact 128-thread tiling was the fastest at 0.00089008 s; compact 160-, 192-, 224-, and 256-thread variants measured about 0.000920–0.000928 s. Prior descriptions retained both CTA barriers. Keep the 128-thread CTA and 16-byte source records, but omit the trailing barrier only after the final tile, when no lane will overwrite shared memory. This tests whether removing that redundant synchronization helps; any benefit is expected to be small and is not assumed.

memory_lessons.applicability: For this source-tiling experiment, compare synchronization costs at the measured best tile size before further widening the CTA.
memory_lessons.claim: The measured compact 128-thread tile was faster than the compact 160-, 192-, 224-, and 256-thread variants in the supplied trials; the results do not establish that larger tiles are better.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure this final-tile barrier omission against the same 128-thread compact staging under the official protocol.

data.notes: The 2,048-byte shared-memory allocation holds one compact source tile. All lanes participate in the start barrier for every tile; the conditional end barrier is uniform across the CTA and is retained whenever another tile follows. Historical measurements are controller observations; this candidate has not been measured or correctness-validated.
transformations: Set block and items_per_block to 128 with 2,048 bytes of dynamic shared memory for 128 compact 16-byte source records.
Assign one target to each thread; stage sources in ascending order and handle partial source tiles and out-of-range target lanes.
Keep the barrier before consuming each tile, but omit the trailing barrier after the final tile because no subsequent tile overwrites shared memory.
